When you write `a + b` and `a` is an `int`, the compiler knows what to do.
When `a` is a `Fraction` you wrote this morning, it does not, and it says so:

```
error: no match for 'operator+' (operand types are 'Fraction' and 'Fraction')
```

**Operator overloading** is how you teach it. You write a function whose name
is `operator+`, and from then on `a + b` calls it. That is the whole idea. What
follows is every operator worth overloading, one at a time, with the exact
signature to copy, the way it looks in a `.h` and a `.cpp`, and the mistake
people make with each one.

The two files everything on this page comes from:
[`Fraction.h`](code/Fraction.h) / [`Fraction.cpp`](code/Fraction.cpp) (a value
type, no heap) and [`Bag.h`](code/Bag.h) / [`Bag.cpp`](code/Bag.cpp) (a class
that owns memory). There is a [`makefile`](code/makefile) and a
[`tests.cpp`](code/tests.cpp) too, so you can clone the folder and break things.

::: {.callout-important}
## The one rule

An overloaded operator should do what a reader who has never seen your class
would guess it does. `a + b` adds. `a == b` says whether they are equal.
`cout << a` prints. If you catch yourself making `+` remove something because
it was convenient, write a method with a name instead.
:::

---

## What the compiler actually does

`a + b` is rewritten into a function call. The compiler tries **two** spellings
and uses whichever one exists:

```cpp
a + b            // what you write

a.operator+(b)   // spelling 1: a METHOD of a's class
operator+(a, b)  // spelling 2: a FREE FUNCTION taking both
```

That is the entire mechanism, and it explains every rule below. A method gets
the left operand as `*this` and the right operand as its parameter. A free
function gets both as parameters. Nothing else is different.

---

## Method or free function?

Most operators can be written either way. Some cannot.

| Operator | Where it must live | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `=`, `[]`, `()`, `->` | **Method**, always | The language says so. |
| `<<`, `>>` | **Free function**, always | The left operand is `cout` or `cin`, not your object, and you cannot add methods to `ostream`. |
| `2 + f` (your type on the *right*) | **Free function** | Spelling 1 would need `2.operator+(f)`, and `int` has no methods. |
| `+`, `-`, `==`, `<`, `++`, unary `-` ... | Either | In CS112, prefer the **method** when the left operand is your class. |
| `.`, `::`, `?:`, `sizeof`, `.*` | **Cannot be overloaded** | Not a design choice you get to make. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[28,24,48]"}

One more thing you cannot do: invent new operators, or change the precedence
of existing ones. `a + b * c` multiplies first whether or not you wrote them.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The CS112 default

When the left operand is your class, write a `const` method. When it is not,
write a free function that goes through the public getters. Reach for `friend`
only when the getters genuinely cannot express what the function needs, and
say why in a comment. (The bottom of this page has a note on `friend`.)
:::

---

## The running example: `Fraction`

Here is the header. Everything below refers back to it, so skim it now and
come back as needed.

```cpp
/* Fraction.h, CS112 operator overloading cheatsheet
 * Calvin University · Fall 2026
 *
 * A fraction with an integer numerator and denominator, kept in
 * lowest terms with a positive denominator. Every operator on
 * this page is declared here and defined in Fraction.cpp.
 */

#ifndef FRACTION_H
#define FRACTION_H

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Fraction {
public:
    Fraction();                               // 0/1
    Fraction(int numerator, int denominator); // throws invalid_argument

    int getNumerator() const;
    int getDenominator() const;

    // arithmetic: a new Fraction, neither operand changes
    Fraction operator+(const Fraction& rhs) const;
    Fraction operator-(const Fraction& rhs) const;
    Fraction operator*(const Fraction& rhs) const;
    Fraction operator/(const Fraction& rhs) const;  // throws

    // compound assignment: this object changes, then hands
    // itself back
    Fraction& operator+=(const Fraction& rhs);

    // unary minus: -f
    Fraction operator-() const;

    // comparison
    bool operator==(const Fraction& rhs) const;
    bool operator!=(const Fraction& rhs) const;
    bool operator< (const Fraction& rhs) const;
    bool operator> (const Fraction& rhs) const;
    bool operator<=(const Fraction& rhs) const;
    bool operator>=(const Fraction& rhs) const;

    // increment: ++f adds one and hands back this object,
    //            f++ adds one and hands back a copy of the
    //            OLD value
    Fraction  operator++(int);   // postfix, the int is a dummy
    Fraction& operator++();      // prefix

    // conversion: (double)f, explicit so it never happens
    // by accident
    explicit operator double() const;

private:
    int myNumerator;
    int myDenominator;

    void reduce();               // lowest terms, positive denom.
};

// stream operators are free functions: the left operand is
// the stream
ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const Fraction& f);
istream& operator>>(istream& in, Fraction& f);   // reads "3/4"

// mixed arithmetic where the Fraction is on the RIGHT: 2 + f
Fraction operator+(int lhs, const Fraction& rhs);

#endif
```

Two things to notice before the operators themselves. Every method that does
not change the object is marked `const`, so it can be called on a
`const Fraction`. And every parameter is `const Fraction&`: a reference, so
nothing is copied, and `const`, so the function promises not to touch it.
Those two habits are what most of the pitfalls below come down to.

---

## 1. Output and input: `<<` and `>>`

You met this one in week 03. It is a **free function**, because the left
operand is the stream, and it **returns the stream** so that the next `<<`
in the chain has something to work on.

```cpp
// Fraction.cpp
ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const Fraction& f) {
    out << f.getNumerator() << "/" << f.getDenominator();
    return out;                  // hand the stream back to chain
}
```

```cpp
Fraction a(1, 2);
cout << a << endl;               // 1/2
cout << "a is " << a << ", done" << endl;
```

Input is the mirror image. The object is **not** `const` (you are filling it
in), and you only change it if the read succeeded:

```cpp
istream& operator>>(istream& in, Fraction& f) {
    int  numerator, denominator;
    char slash;
    in >> numerator >> slash >> denominator;
    if (in) {                    // only change f if the read worked
        f = Fraction(numerator, denominator);
    }
    return in;
}
```

```cpp
Fraction f;
cin >> f;                        // type 3/9, get 1/3
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The two ways this goes wrong

**Returning `void`.** Then `cout << a` works but `cout << a << endl` does not,
because `(cout << a)` is now nothing and nothing has no `<<`.

**Making it a method.** `f << cout` is what a method would give you, since
`*this` is the left operand. Nobody writes that. If you want to keep the
printing logic inside the class, give the class a `writeTo(ostream&)` method
and have the free `operator<<` call it.
:::

---

## 2. Arithmetic: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`

A **`const` method** that builds a **new** object and returns it **by value**.
Neither operand changes. This is what `+` on `int` does, so it is what `+` on
`Fraction` should do.

```cpp
Fraction Fraction::operator+(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    int numerator   = myNumerator * rhs.myDenominator
                    + rhs.myNumerator * myDenominator;
    int denominator = myDenominator * rhs.myDenominator;
    return Fraction(numerator, denominator);  // constructor reduces
}

Fraction Fraction::operator*(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    return Fraction(myNumerator * rhs.myNumerator,
                    myDenominator * rhs.myDenominator);
}

Fraction Fraction::operator/(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    if (rhs.myNumerator == 0) {
        throw invalid_argument("cannot divide by zero");
    }
    return Fraction(myNumerator * rhs.myDenominator,
                    myDenominator * rhs.myNumerator);
}
```

Inside a method of `Fraction`, `rhs.myNumerator` is allowed even though
`myNumerator` is private. Privacy is per **class**, not per object: any
`Fraction` code can see any `Fraction`'s insides.

Once one operator works, define the others in terms of it rather than
starting over:

```cpp
Fraction Fraction::operator-(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    return *this + (-rhs);       // reuse + and unary -
}
```

```cpp
Fraction a(1, 2), b(3, 4);
Fraction c = a + b;              // 5/4, and a and b are unchanged
cout << a - b << " " << a * b << " " << a / b << endl;
                                 // -1/4 3/8 2/3
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Forgetting `const` on the method

Without the trailing `const`, this does not compile:

```cpp
const Fraction half(1, 2);
Fraction one = half + half;      // error: passing 'const Fraction'
                                 //  as 'this' discards qualifiers
```

A `const` object may only call `const` methods. Since `+` does not change
the left operand, it should have been `const` from the start. (This is the
mistake in a well-known online cheatsheet. Now you know why it is a mistake.)
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Returning a reference to a local

```cpp
Fraction& Fraction::operator+(const Fraction& rhs) const {  // NO
    Fraction result(...);
    return result;               // result dies here
}
```

`result` lives on the stack of this call. The reference outlives it. Return
arithmetic results **by value**. The copy is cheap and the compiler usually
removes it anyway.
:::

### When your type is on the right: `2 + f`

`2 + f` would need `2.operator+(f)`, and `int` has no methods. So this one is
a **free function**, and it can be one line if the constructor and the method
already exist:

```cpp
// The Fraction is on the right, so this cannot be a method
Fraction operator+(int lhs, const Fraction& rhs) {
    return Fraction(lhs, 1) + rhs;
}
```

```cpp
Fraction a(1, 2);
cout << 2 + a << endl;           // 5/2
```

---

## 3. Compound assignment: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`

These **change the left operand** and then hand it back, so `a += b` can sit
inside a bigger expression the way it can for `int`. The return type is a
**reference to `*this`**, and the method is **not** `const` because it
changes the object.

```cpp
Fraction& Fraction::operator+=(const Fraction& rhs) {
    *this = *this + rhs;         // reuse +, then hand this object back
    return *this;
}
```

```cpp
Fraction c(1, 4);
c += Fraction(1, 2);             // c is now 3/4
```

Either `+` is written in terms of `+=`, or `+=` in terms of `+`. Pick one.
Never write the arithmetic twice.

---

## 4. Unary minus: `-f`

Same name as subtraction, but **no parameter**. That is how the compiler tells
`-f` (one operand) from `a - f` (two). It is `const` and returns a new value.

```cpp
Fraction Fraction::operator-() const {
    return Fraction(-myNumerator, myDenominator);
}
```

```cpp
Fraction a(1, 2);
cout << -a << endl;              // -1/2
```

`!` and unary `+` work the same way: `bool operator!() const`, no parameter.

---

## 5. Comparison: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`

`const` methods returning `bool`. The trick is to write **two** of them with
real logic and derive the other four, so there is one place for a bug to
live.

```cpp
bool Fraction::operator==(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    // both are in lowest terms, so equal fractions have equal parts
    return myNumerator == rhs.myNumerator
        && myDenominator == rhs.myDenominator;
}

bool Fraction::operator<(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    // denominators are positive, so cross-multiplying keeps
    // the direction
    return myNumerator * rhs.myDenominator
         < rhs.myNumerator * myDenominator;
}

// the other four, in terms of those two
bool Fraction::operator!=(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    return !(*this == rhs);
}
bool Fraction::operator>(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    return rhs < *this;
}
bool Fraction::operator<=(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    return !(rhs < *this);
}
bool Fraction::operator>=(const Fraction& rhs) const {
    return !(*this < rhs);
}
```

```cpp
Fraction a(1, 2), b(3, 4);
REQUIRE(Fraction(2, 4) == a);    // 2/4 reduced to 1/2
REQUIRE(a != b);
REQUIRE(a < b);
REQUIRE(b > a);
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why `==` matters more than it looks

Catch's `REQUIRE(x == y)` needs `operator==`. So does `std::find`. Later in
the semester `std::set` and `std::map` will need `operator<` to order your
type. Write these two early, in the `.h`, and every tool downstream starts
working.
:::

---

## 6. Increment and decrement: `++f` and `f++`

Two operators that look identical. C++ tells them apart with a **dummy `int`
parameter** that is never used: the version with the `int` is postfix.

```cpp
Fraction& Fraction::operator++() {         // ++f, prefix
    myNumerator += myDenominator;          // add 1 = d/d
    return *this;                          // the changed object
}

Fraction Fraction::operator++(int) {       // f++, postfix
    Fraction old = *this;                  // remember the old value
    ++(*this);                             // reuse the prefix version
    return old;                            // hand back the OLD value
}
```

```cpp
Fraction d(1, 3);
cout << ++d << " ";              // 4/3   (changed, then printed)
cout << d++ << " ";              // 4/3   (printed, then changed)
cout << d   << endl;             // 7/3
```

Prefix returns a **reference** (the object itself, already changed). Postfix
returns a **copy** (the value from before the change), so it cannot return a
reference and it costs a copy. That is the same reason `++i` is preferred
over `i++` in a `for` loop when it makes no difference to the logic.

`--` is identical with `-=`.

---

## 7. Conversion: `(double) f`

A conversion operator lets your object turn into another type. It has **no
return type in the signature** (the name *is* the type) and no parameters.

```cpp
Fraction::operator double() const {
    return (double) myNumerator / myDenominator;
}
```

```cpp
Fraction a(1, 2);
double x = (double) a;           // 0.5
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Make it `explicit`

The header says `explicit operator double() const;`. Without `explicit`, the
compiler is allowed to convert a `Fraction` to a `double` **silently**,
wherever a `double` fits: `a + 1.5` would become `0.5 + 1.5` instead of a
compile error, and `if (a)` would quietly test whether the value is nonzero.
`explicit` means the conversion only happens when you write the cast. That is
the version to copy.
:::

---

## 8. Subscript: `bag[i]`

From here on the example is `Bag`, a class that owns an array on the heap:

```cpp
class Bag {
public:
    Bag(unsigned size);                  // size zeros
    Bag(const Bag& original);            // deep copy
    ~Bag();
    Bag& operator=(const Bag& rhs);      // deep copy, self-safe

    unsigned getSize() const;

    // subscript, one for reading a const Bag, one for changing
    int&       operator[](unsigned i);          // throws
    const int& operator[](unsigned i) const;    // throws

    // call operator: bag(k) counts how many items equal k
    unsigned operator()(int value) const;

private:
    int*     myItems;
    unsigned mySize;
};

ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const Bag& bag);
```

`[]` **must be a method**. You write it **twice**: once returning a plain
reference so `bag[i] = 7` can change the item, and once as a `const` method
returning a `const` reference so a `const Bag` can still be read.

```cpp
int& Bag::operator[](unsigned i) {
    if (i >= mySize) {
        throw range_error("no item at that index");
    }
    return myItems[i];                   // a reference: bag[i] = 7
}

const int& Bag::operator[](unsigned i) const {
    if (i >= mySize) {
        throw range_error("no item at that index");
    }
    return myItems[i];                   // read only
}
```

```cpp
Bag bag(3);
bag[0] = 7;                      // the non-const one, returns int&
const Bag copy = bag;
cout << copy[0] << endl;         // the const one, returns const int&
bag[5] = 1;                      // throws range_error
```

Yes, the two bodies are identical. That is normal for `[]`. The compiler picks
the one that matches whether the object is `const`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two things not to do inside `[]`

**Print an error and `exit`.** A container's job is to hold things, not to
end the program. Throw `range_error` and let the caller decide. Your tests can
then say `REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(bag[5], range_error)`, which they cannot do with
`exit`.

**Only write the non-const version.** Then `operator<<`, which takes a
`const Bag&`, cannot use `bag[i]` and you are back to reaching inside the
class. Write both.
:::

---

## 9. Assignment: `a = b`

This is the one operator the compiler writes **for you** if you do not, and
for `Fraction` that default is fine: it copies each member, which is all a
`Fraction` needs. Notice `Fraction.h` does not declare an `operator=` at all.

For `Bag` the default is a bug. It would copy the **pointer**, so two `Bag`s
end up sharing one array, and the second destructor to run deletes memory the
first already freed. So `Bag` writes its own, and the shape is always the
same four steps:

```cpp
Bag& Bag::operator=(const Bag& rhs) {
    if (this != &rhs) {                  // 1. guard: b = b;
        delete[] myItems;                // 2. let go of the old array
        mySize  = rhs.mySize;
        myItems = new int[rhs.mySize];   // 3. get a new one and fill it
        for (unsigned i = 0; i < mySize; i++) {
            myItems[i] = rhs.myItems[i];
        }
    }
    return *this;                        // 4. so a = b = c works
}
```

```cpp
Bag a(3), b(1);
a[0] = 7;
b = a;                           // b now has its own copy of a's array
b = b;                           // harmless, thanks to the guard
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The rule of three

If a class needs any one of a **destructor**, a **copy constructor**, or a
**copy assignment operator**, it needs all three, and for the same reason: it
owns something. `Bag` has all three. `Fraction` has none of them. If you find
yourself writing just one, stop and ask what the other two would do.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Why step 1 exists

Without the self-assignment guard, `b = b` runs step 2 first and deletes the
array, then step 3 reads from `rhs.myItems`, which is the array it just
deleted. `b = b` looks silly written out, but `bags[i] = bags[j]` with
`i == j` is not silly at all.
:::

---

## 10. Call: `bag(7)`

Overloading `()` makes an object **callable like a function**. An object that
does this is called a **functor**. It must be a method, it can take any
parameters you like, and it is how you hand behaviour plus state to something
that expects a function, which is exactly what the STL's sort and search
functions will want from you later.

```cpp
unsigned Bag::operator()(int value) const {
    unsigned count = 0;
    for (unsigned i = 0; i < mySize; i++) {
        if (myItems[i] == value) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}
```

```cpp
Bag bag(3);
bag[0] = 7; bag[1] = 7; bag[2] = 2;
cout << bag(7) << endl;          // 2, the object was "called"
```

Use this one sparingly. `bag.count(7)` says the same thing and needs no
explanation. `()` earns its place when the object is going to be handed to
code that only knows how to call things.

---

## Putting it together: `operator<<` for `Bag`

The stream operator for `Bag` uses two other overloads on this page, and it
uses them from the **outside**, through the public interface:

```cpp
ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const Bag& bag) {
    out << "[";
    for (unsigned i = 0; i < bag.getSize(); i++) {
        if (i > 0) {
            out << ", ";
        }
        out << bag[i];                   // the const operator[]
    }
    out << "]";
    return out;
}
```

`bag` is a `const Bag&`, so `bag[i]` picks the `const` subscript. That is the
payoff for writing it twice.

---

## The signature table

Copy from here. `T` is your class.

| Operator | Kind | Signature | Returns | `const`? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cout << t` | free | `ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const T& t)` | the stream | n/a |
| `cin >> t` | free | `istream& operator>>(istream& in, T& t)` | the stream | n/a |
| `t + u` | method | `T operator+(const T& rhs) const` | new value | yes |
| `2 + t` | free | `T operator+(int lhs, const T& rhs)` | new value | n/a |
| `t += u` | method | `T& operator+=(const T& rhs)` | `*this` | no |
| `-t` | method | `T operator-() const` | new value | yes |
| `t == u` | method | `bool operator==(const T& rhs) const` | `bool` | yes |
| `t < u` | method | `bool operator<(const T& rhs) const` | `bool` | yes |
| `++t` | method | `T& operator++()` | `*this` | no |
| `t++` | method | `T operator++(int)` | old value | no |
| `(double) t` | method | `explicit operator double() const` | `double` | yes |
| `t[i]` | method | `Item& operator[](unsigned i)` | reference | no |
| `t[i]` on `const` | method | `const Item& operator[](unsigned i) const` | const ref | yes |
| `t = u` | method | `T& operator=(const T& rhs)` | `*this` | no |
| `t(x)` | method | `R operator()(Args) const` | whatever | usually |

: {tbl-colwidths="[13,9,50,15,13]"}

The pattern in the last column: **if the operator changes the object, it is
not `const` and it returns `*this` by reference. If it does not, it is `const`
and it returns a new value.**

---

## A note on `friend`

Some books write `operator<<` like this:

```cpp
class Fraction {
    friend ostream& operator<<(ostream& out, const Fraction& f);
    ...
};
```

`friend` lets a free function read the private members directly, so the body
can say `f.myNumerator` instead of `f.getNumerator()`. It works, and you will
see it in the wild. In CS112 we do not use it by default, because a class
with getters does not need it, and every `friend` is one more piece of code
that breaks when the private section changes. If a function genuinely cannot
do its job through the public interface, that is usually a sign the public
interface is missing something.

---

## Checklist before you hand it in

- Every operator that does not change the object is a **`const` method**.
- Every parameter of a class type is **`const T&`**, not `T`.
- `<<` and `>>` are **free functions** that **return the stream**.
- Arithmetic returns **by value**; compound assignment and prefix `++` return
  **`*this` by reference**; postfix `++` has the **dummy `int`** and returns
  the **old value**.
- `[]` comes in **two versions**, and both **throw** on a bad index.
- If the class has a destructor, it has a **copy constructor** and an
  **`operator=`** with the **self-assignment guard**.
- Conversions are **`explicit`**.
- Every operator has a **test**. `REQUIRE(a + b == c)` is one line.
